title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 13
topics: Public space and the shape of cities

part1.topic: Places to relax near where you live
questions: Where do you usually go when you want to unwind near your home?
Do you go there alone, or is it somewhere you take people?
Is it somewhere you visit regularly, or only when you really need a break?
Have the relaxing places in your area changed since you were a child?
If you could add one relaxing place to your neighbourhood, what would it be?
How much walking do you do in a normal day?
Do you ever walk somewhere when you could easily take transport instead? Why?
Is your area a pleasant place to walk around, or not really?
Did you walk more at some earlier point in your life than you do now?
Do you think people in your country will walk more or less in the coming years?

part2.title: Describe a public place where you enjoy spending time.
bullets: where this place is and what it looks like
how often you go there and what you do there
what kinds of people you see there
how the place makes you feel
part2.explain: and explain why you keep going back to this place rather than somewhere else.
followups: Is it busier at certain times of day?
Would you miss it if it closed or disappeared?
Do your friends or family like it as much as you do?

part3.q: What makes a public place genuinely pleasant to spend time in?
followups: Is it mainly about design, or about the people?
Can a busy place still be relaxing?

part3.q: Many cities seem designed around cars rather than people. Why did that happen?
followups: Is it being reversed where you live?
Who loses most in a car-first city?

part3.q: Some cities are now removing traffic from their centres entirely. Do you think that's the right direction?
followups: What about the people who depend on driving?
Would it work in the cities of your country?

part3.q: Who should pay for parks and public squares — everyone through taxes, or mainly the people who use them?
followups: Is a park a luxury or a necessity?
What happens to public places when nobody wants to fund them?

part3.q: Shopping malls now serve as gathering places in many cities. Is a mall a real substitute for a public square?
followups: What's the difference between space that's public and space that's merely open to the public?
Does it matter who is quietly excluded from a mall?

part3.q: How much difference does access to green space actually make to people's wellbeing?
followups: Is that need stronger now than in the past?
Should there be a legal right to live near a park?

part3.q: In many cities, the poorest neighbourhoods have the least public space. Why does that pattern keep appearing?
followups: Whose job is it to fix that?
Does anything change when it is fixed?

part3.q: Does the design of a public place change how strangers behave towards each other?
followups: Can you think of a place that brings out the best in people?
And one that does the opposite?

part3.q: With shopping and work moving online, what do you think city centres will actually be for in twenty years?
followups: Is that a decline or just a change?
What would make people keep showing up in person?

part3.q: If a city could invest heavily in either public transport or public space, but not both, which should come first?
followups: Are the two really separable?
Would your answer differ for a small town?

fc: Sustains two minutes on a single place by moving through registers — physical description, routine, people-watching, feeling — rather than repeating "it's very peaceful" in new orders.
Part 1 answers about walking and relaxing flow at natural length: two to four sentences, always with a reason or detail attached.
In Part 3, builds the city-design answers as small arguments — claim, reason, example — instead of piling up disconnected observations.
Handles the either/or investment question decisively: picks, defends, concedes the cost, and doesn't stall in "both are important".
Description never stalls the clock: even while picturing the place, the speech keeps moving with natural fillers of substance ("the thing you notice first is…").
lr: Place vocabulary that goes beyond 'beautiful': leafy, run-down, tucked away, bustling, a bit of a sun-trap, well kept, on its last legs.
Urban Part 3 lexis used accurately: pedestrianised, green belt, amenities, footfall, gentrification, accessible — without turning into a planning textbook.
Distinguishes public, communal, shared and open-to-the-public — a distinction one Part 3 question explicitly hunts for.
People-watching language for the third bullet: regulars, dog-walkers, chess players, young families, older men who seem to live on that bench.
Feeling vocabulary with gradation: at ease, recharged, oddly anonymous, part of something — not just 'relaxed' four times.
gra: Present habitual structures carry the routine bullets: "I tend to go on Sunday mornings", "I'll usually grab a coffee and just watch".
Spatial description under control: "there's a fountain in the middle, with plane trees running along both sides, and behind that a row of food stalls".
Passives arrive naturally in the city questions: "the centre was pedestrianised a few years ago", "parks are being sold off for development".
Second conditionals for the policy questions: "If parking were pushed underground, the square would breathe again."
Comparatives and superlatives stay accurate under speed: "far livelier than", "one of the few places where", "the greener the street, the slower people walk".
pron: Descriptive stretches get varied intonation — flat delivery kills a two-minute description faster than any grammar slip.
Stress carries the key contrast of this test: "public space" versus "private space", "designed for cars" versus "designed for people".
Place-name pronunciation is confident; hesitating over your own city's districts undermines an otherwise fluent description.
The /w/ in walk and the vowel in park, calm, square are clear — this topic set leans on exactly those sounds.
Lists of what you see there — "joggers, vendors, kids on bikes" — use natural list rhythm rather than identical stress on every item.

band9.part1: Answer, then anchor it in one specific image from your real life. For "Where do you usually go when you want to unwind near your home?" a Band 9 answer names a real spot with texture: "There's a small lake about ten minutes' walk from my flat — nothing spectacular, but there's one bench on the far side that catches the evening sun, and that bench is basically my therapist." One concrete image beats three general sentences about how relaxation is important for health.
part2: Name and place it immediately — "the riverside promenade in my city", "the courtyard of the old library" — then give two or three visual details that let the examiner see it: what's at the centre, what's around the edges, what you hear.

Cover the routine bullet with habits, not statistics — "most Saturday mornings, and the odd weekday evening when work has been heavy" sounds human; "I visit it 2–3 times per week" sounds like a report.
Do the people bullet as a small gallery — three or four types you actually see there, sketched in a phrase each; this bullet is a gift for vocabulary and most candidates skip it entirely.
Give the feeling bullet a mechanism — not just "it makes me feel calm" but why: the anonymity, the water, the fact that nobody there wants anything from you.
Add one specific memory — a single small scene (a festival evening, a conversation with a stranger, the first visit) to break the description's present tense and show narrative range.
Close on the explain line — why this place and not somewhere else: name the alternative you don't choose and what the winner has that it lacks.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Shopping malls now serve as gathering places in many cities. Is a mall a real substitute for a public square?
framework: Answer: take the position — no, not fully, because a mall is open to the public but not owned by it, and that difference shapes everything inside.

Explain: give the mechanism — a mall exists to sell, so every bench, camera and rule filters for people who might spend; a square tolerates you whether you buy anything or not, and that unconditional welcome is the point of public space.

Example: make it concrete — in fierce summers people do treat air-conditioned malls as the town square, yet teenagers get moved on by security for simply lingering, which would be absurd in an actual square.

Alternative view: concede honestly — malls are safe, clean, cool and accessible, and where cities have neglected real squares, the mall is a rational refuge rather than a mistake by the people who gather there.

Evaluate: land the judgement — the mall is a substitute the way a rented room is a substitute for a home: it works until you break a rule; cities that let it become the only option have quietly privatised their common life.

mistakes.title: Choosing a private place for a public-place card
mistakes.detail: Your bedroom, a friend's café table, your gym — candidates regularly pick places that aren't public, then have nothing to say for the 'kinds of people you see there' bullet. Parks, squares, markets, riversides and libraries all fit; your sofa doesn't.

mistakes.title: Describing the place without yourself in it
mistakes.detail: The card is about a place where you spend time — your routine, your bench, your reasons. A tourist-brochure description of the park's features, however fluent, leaves two of the four bullets untouched.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the people-watching bullet
mistakes.detail: "What kinds of people you see there" is the easiest bullet to develop and the most skipped. A one-line gallery — joggers at dawn, chess players by the gate, families at weekends — adds thirty seconds of natural, high-scoring description.

mistakes.title: Repeating 'relaxing' until it wears out
mistakes.detail: This test invites the word constantly. Rotate the language: unwind, switch off, clear my head, recharge, take the edge off the day. Ten 'relaxing's in two minutes is a visible vocabulary ceiling.

mistakes.title: Turning Part 3 into a pollution essay
mistakes.detail: The car-versus-people questions sit near the memorised 'environment' topic, and candidates swerve into exhaust fumes and global warming. These questions are about space, design and who streets are for — pollution is one thread, not the answer.

mistakes.title: Answering the funding question with 'the government should pay'
mistakes.detail: That's the start of a position, not a whole one. Who is the government, if not taxpayers? Band 8–9 answers see the real question — whether non-users should subsidise users — and take a view on it.

mistakes.title: Missing the mall question's trap
mistakes.detail: It isn't asking whether malls are nice. It's probing whether privately owned space can do a public square's job. Candidates who catch the ownership point — who's welcome, who's quietly excluded — immediately sound a band higher.

mistakes.title: Vague geography in Part 2
mistakes.detail: "It is a park in my city, it is very big, there are many trees" could describe ten thousand parks. Named streets, the market next door, the specific bench — verifiable-sounding detail is what makes description convincing and keeps it flowing.

mistakes.title: Treating the future-of-city-centres question as pure guesswork
mistakes.detail: "Nobody can know the future" is a refusal to play. The evidence is already visible — empty shops, streets converted to seating, events replacing retail. Read the trend you can see, then project it; that's all the question wants.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the explain line entirely
mistakes.detail: "Why you keep going back rather than somewhere else" begs for a comparison, and most candidates never name the somewhere else. One sentence — "the newer park is closer, but it's all concrete and noise" — answers the card's hardest part in one move.
